title: Object literals
description: Object literals — shorthand properties, computed keys, method shorthand, and dot vs bracket access.

notes: Dot access requires a literal identifier; bracket access takes any expression.
Computed keys [expr] run at object-creation time; the result is coerced to a string (or Symbol).
Method shorthand defines a normal function — `this` refers to the object when called as obj.method().

questions.q: What does `{ name }` expand to when name is a variable holding "Ada"?
Given `const k = "x"`, which literal sets key "x" to 1?
When MUST you use bracket access instead of dot?
options: When the key is in a variable or not a valid identifier
When the value is an object

exercises.prompt: Build a user object using shorthand properties.

blanks.hint: same identifier as the variable — that IS the shorthand

exercises.prompt: Use a computed key driven by a variable.

blanks.hint: the variable that holds the key name

L3.prompt: Write `makeUser(name, age)` returning an object with shorthand properties and a method `greet()` returning "hi " + this.name. Log `makeUser("Ada", 36).greet()`.
hints: Shorthand: { name, age } takes values from same-named variables.
Method shorthand: greet() { ... } — no function keyword.
